title: L-417 is on in daylight
action: Open on actual Command Center L-417 anomaly. Frame On, daylight, schedule Off. Overlay: Local simulation / Unit 00 pilot. No title slide first.
verify: Cold-open footage must come from this run, with the healthy Lights On fixture.
narration: This streetlight is on in daylight. The schedule says it should be off. You are the operator: can you restore it, and prove that the command actually worked? In this unit, you will start the Caesarea lab, repair L four seventeen, check the result at the Energy Hub, and reset the incident so you can repeat it. The streetlight is simulated. The services and commands you will inspect are real local execution.

title: What success will look like
action: Hold a readable close view of reported, desired, schedule, override and controller state. Identify evidence without clicking restore.
verify: Do not present the manual override as proof of a technician's reason.
narration: Success is more than a green screen. We want the Hub to report that the lamp is off, the manual override is cleared, and the last command succeeded after confirmation from the simulator. We will also inspect the command's correlation identifier. Right now, the override tells us a condition of the system. It does not tell us why somebody left the light on. That distinction will matter when we add the Operations Agent and investigate the cause in later lessons.

title: Where intelligence belongs
action: Use H08 p15 briefly; return attention to the single incident. Credit Alon Fliess. No catalogue of features.
verify: Explicitly say Unit00 runs no model; identify observation, inference and authority separately.
narration: Microsoft Agent Framework gives our C sharp application agents, tools, sessions, and workflows. An agent can choose what to inspect next when the evidence changes the investigation. But the known repair path we need today is deterministic. We do not need a model to restore a schedule. The companion book starts with this architectural choice: use the least autonomy that solves the requirement. Later, the agent will observe through tools and infer an explanation. Permission to change city state still belongs at an enforced service boundary.

title: Two screens, two responsibilities
action: Use the architecture visual, followed by Director and main-app captures when editing. Point to the Energy Hub and SmartPole boundary.
verify: Describe SmartPole as a simulator and distinguish preparation from operation.
narration: There are two browser surfaces. Demo Director is our lab bench: it creates the starting conditions and selects a stage. Command Center is the operator's application: that is where we perform the repair. Behind it, the Command Center API calls the Energy Hub, and only the Hub talks to SmartPole. SmartPole simulates the physical device. We will read the Hub directly to check what the operational system knows, rather than treating the browser's presentation as independent proof.

title: Prepare the starting fixture
action: Click Director 1 Deterministic, show preparation preview, confirm, then show readiness. Capture the actual interaction sequence.
verify: Lights On Reported by a Client / ForgottenOverride, Deterministic, healthy controller.
narration: In the Director, choose beat one, Deterministic. Read the preparation preview before confirming. We want Lights On Reported by a Client, which the code calls Forgotten Override. These names refer to the same starting fixture. The stage decides which capabilities are available; the scenario decides the condition of the city. Confirm preparation and check readiness. If you previously repaired the light, explicitly reapply this scenario. Merely selecting a stage that is already active does not prove that you recreated the anomaly.

title: Read the operator's facts
action: Switch to Command Center. Read L-417, North Promenade, customer report, On, Off schedule, override, healthy controller.
verify: No agent question or cloud result is implied; facts match fresh Hub read next.
narration: Switch to Command Center. Find L four seventeen on the North Promenade. Read the customer report and the operational fields before touching the action. The lamp is reported on, it is daylight, the schedule expects off, and the override is active. The controller is healthy. At this stage we have no agent investigation. The system can detect the discrepancy and execute a predefined correction. It cannot explain the maintenance decision merely because we gave the scenario a suggestive name.

title: Check the Energy Hub before acting
action: Execute lab step4 in a second terminal; show the actual selected fields and save before snapshot. Copy the Hub URL from Aspire.
verify: Actual JSON: reportedIsOn true, expectedScheduledState false, manualOverride true; retain real revision.
narration: Now make the independent check. In a second terminal, set hub base to the HTTPS Energy Hub address from Aspire, then run the read command in the lab. This calls the Hub's asset endpoint for L four seventeen. Compare reported state, schedule, override, and revision with the browser. Store this response as before. The revision is a version of authoritative state, not a value you should copy from my recording. Our read has its own correlation identifier; the repair will have another one. We will use the repair identifier when joining its events.

title: Restore scheduled mode
action: Record the actual Command Center click Restore Scheduled Mode and its pending/completed transition. Preserve meaningful wait; label any cut.
verify: Command is issued from main UI, not secretly from a test/API script substituted for this shot.
narration: Return to Command Center and click Restore Scheduled Mode once. Watch the request complete. The operator is initiating a narrow deterministic operation. There is no model deciding whether to press the button, and no claim here of a production identity deployment. The Hub computes the target, sends the device command, and waits for a result. A desired target can change while that work is pending. We must wait for confirmation before saying that the reported lamp state has changed.

title: Verify the receipt and reported state
action: Execute lab step5 read/assertions. Show actual lastCommand and correlated activity. Hold readable fields; no invented receipt or fixed timestamp.
verify: Reported/desired/override false; receipt Succeeded; newer revision; matching correlation and simulator confirmation.
narration: Read the Hub again. The expected outcome is reported off, desired off, and manual override false. Inspect last command: it must say Succeeded, with a completion time and a correlation identifier. Check that the revision advanced from the snapshot you saved. Then filter the Hub activity by this command's identifier and read the confirmation. The lab includes checks that fail if these conditions are missing. This combination is our evidence. The browser changing color, or an HTTP request being accepted, would not be enough. We have proven the local simulated repair, not delivery to a real streetlight.

title: Why this code waits for confirmation
action: Readable actual EnergyHubService.cs excerpt, RestoreScheduledModeAsync: SetLampStateAsync and success branch. Show filename and real line numbers.
verify: Excerpt taken from clean baseline; emphasize actual reported-state assignment after succeeded confirmation.
narration: Open Energy Hub Service dot cs, in Restore Scheduled Mode Async. Look at the call to Set Lamp State Async and the success branch immediately after it. Reported Is On is assigned from the confirmed device result, and the override is cleared there. Earlier in the method, a pending command can record the desired target without inventing a reported success. This is why the Energy Hub remains the operational authority even after we add an agent. The agent may propose or request work; a confident explanation cannot replace this confirmation boundary.

title: A repair is not an investigation
action: Return to completed main UI; briefly highlight absence of a newly established causal explanation.
verify: Do not imply incident closure or evidence-backed diagnosis merely from restore.
narration: Back in Command Center, the lamp is off. We have corrected the condition, but we still have not established the technician's reason. In the next lessons, the Operations Agent will read current state, follow the conversation, and retrieve a work order. That work order can be evidence. A similar remembered incident is only a lead to investigate. Keeping those categories separate prevents yesterday's explanation from becoming today's operational truth. The same L four seventeen case will let us see the difference.

action: Show Director reapply Lights On Reported by a Client while Deterministic stays selected. Return to main UI and fresh Hub snapshot.
verify: Actual On/override on restored; acknowledge reset mutates the revision and clears prior command context as implemented.
narration: Before repeating the exercise, reset the lab deliberately. Go back to the Director and reapply Lights On Reported by a Client, with Deterministic still selected. Return to the main app and read the Hub again. The lamp should be on with the override active and the controller healthy. Save a new before snapshot. Do not compare a new repair with a snapshot from an earlier scenario. This visible reset is how we reuse the incident in every lesson without hiding a preparation step from you.

title: Pause and do
action: Exercise card with three short tasks and lab link. Hold a quiet 5-second pause after narration if needed.
verify: Learner repeats prepared fixture, main-app restore and Hub verification independently.
narration: Pause the video now. Starting from the reset fixture, read and save the Hub state. Perform the restore from Command Center. Then verify the Hub's reported state, override, command receipt, and revision without following my clicks. Explain three things out loud: which service owns reported state; what distinguishes accepting a command from completing it; and what you still do not know about the cause. The companion lab contains copyable commands and checkpoints. Take the time you need, then return for the expected result and a recovery tip.

title: Expected result and recovery
action: Show expected-result checklist clearly labeled Expected, alongside earlier verified receipt. Explain wrong-fixture recovery; no fabricated fault run.
verify: A failure case described rather than executed is labeled explanation. Actual receipt remains distinguishable from expectation.
narration: Your answer should name the Energy Hub as owner of the operational twin. Success requires the confirmed off state and a succeeded correlated command, not just a changed desired target. We still need evidence for the cause. If your result differs, check the fixture first. Controller Fault is designed to fail the healthy-device expectation, while Normal Operation is already off. Reapply Lights On Reported by a Client, verify a healthy controller and Deterministic stage, reread the Hub, and retry. Do not keep clicking against an unexplained failed receipt. Inspect it and restore the starting conditions.
